comment: The graded rubric behind the intake coherence check (FR-43). Five criteria scored 1-4 over the WHOLE intake read as one document — coherence is a property of the set, not of any one field. A model assigns levels and nothing else; the band, the wording and the order of the asks are all deterministic and all from this file. Anchors and asks are business copy: edit them here, never in code. See .claude/skills/intake-rubric/SKILL.md for why each criterion exists. It never blocks submission (G-69).

engine.opening: Here is how this reads to a reviewer who has not met you. None of it blocks you — you can submit as it stands and a reviewer will pick up anything thin.

messages.tooShort: That is too thin to work from. A few sentences about what the activity does, what data it touches and who else is involved gives the platform something to route on — and saves you being asked later.
messages.notProse: That does not read as a description yet. The platform routes on what you write, so it needs real sentences about the activity.

bands.label: Robust
bands.meaning: A reviewer can work from this as written.

bands.label: Workable
bands.meaning: Usable. The gaps below are specific and quick to close.

bands.label: Thin
bands.meaning: Routing will be working from guesses in places.

bands.label: Not yet usable
bands.meaning: As written, this cannot be assessed without asking you first.

criteria.label: Clarity & Coherence
criteria.why: Whether a reviewer can determine the purpose at all.

anchors.1: Vague, fragmented, or unintelligible. The core purpose of the project cannot be determined.
anchors.2: Understandable but lacks detail. Uses heavy jargon without context, leaving some ambiguity.
anchors.3: Clear and logical. The reviewer can easily grasp the project's purpose, though minor details may be missing.
anchors.4: Exceptionally clear, well-structured, and precise. Leaves no doubt about the project's exact purpose and functionality.

ask.1: Say what this actually does, in one plain sentence — the specific job, not the category it belongs to.
ask.2: Cut the jargon or explain it. A reviewer who does not work in your area should be able to follow it.
ask.3: Close, and worth one more sentence on the part a stranger would still have to guess at.

criteria.label: Internal Consistency
criteria.why: Whether the answers contradict each other — the one thing a person cannot check for themselves, because they know what they meant.

anchors.1: Major contradictions (for example, states it is an internal app but lists external users later).
anchors.2: Contains minor conflicts or confusing statements that require clarification before approval.
anchors.3: Generally consistent. Facts align throughout with no glaring operational conflicts.
anchors.4: Fully consistent. Technical, business, and user details align with no contradictions.

ask.1: Two of your answers disagree with each other. Both are named below — one of them needs changing.
ask.2: Something here reads two ways. Worth a sentence to settle which you mean.
ask.3: Consistent as far as it goes.

criteria.label: User Audience & Scope
criteria.why: Who uses it, and where it stops.

anchors.1: No mention of who will use the system or the overall business scope.
anchors.2: Mentions users vaguely (for example, "employees"). Scope boundaries are blurry.
anchors.3: Identifies specific user groups (for example, "HR admins") and generally defines what the project will and will not do.
anchors.4: Clearly defines exact user roles, permission levels, and the boundaries of the project's scope.

ask.1: Who actually uses this, and what does it deliberately not do? Both change which questions you are asked.
ask.2: "Employees" could be anyone. Which group — and can they all see everything?
ask.3: Worth naming the permission levels if there is more than one.

criteria.label: Data Access & Flow
criteria.why: Who reaches the data and how it moves. Decides which risk areas open and who reviews it.

anchors.1: Ignores data access entirely. No explanation of how data is accessed, stored, or transferred.
anchors.2: Mentions data access briefly but misses key details like third-party access or data transit methods.
anchors.3: Explains who accesses the data and the general data flow, but may lack specifics on downstream systems.
anchors.4: Fully maps data access, including third-party vendors, APIs, storage locations, and the data lifecycle.

ask.1: Nothing here says who touches the data or where it goes. That decides which risk areas open, so it is the most useful thing you can add.
ask.2: Does anyone outside the organisation see this data, and how does it get to them?
ask.3: Worth naming where it ends up — the downstream systems, not just the first hop.

criteria.label: Data Sensitivity
criteria.why: What kind of data, and how sensitive. Decides the severity questions you are asked.

anchors.1: Fails to mention what type of data the project will handle.
anchors.2: Broadly mentions data but does not classify its sensitivity (for example, "user data" without specifying personal information).
anchors.3: Identifies the general data types and acknowledges whether sensitive data (personal, health, financial) is present.
anchors.4: Explicitly lists the data types, classifies their sensitivity, and notes the compliance requirements that follow.

ask.1: What data does this hold or read? Naming it decides which questions you are asked next.
ask.2: Does any of it identify a person, or count as confidential? That is what changes the assessment.
ask.3: Worth naming the regime if one applies — the reviewer will ask.
